question_en: An investor purchases a bond with 5 years until maturity, a 4% annual coupon payment, and a YTM of 4.25%. The investor holds the bond until maturity. After purchase and before the first coupon, if the YTM for similar bonds increases to 4.5% due to a rise in interest rates and remains at that level for the life of the bond, then the value of the investor's reinvested coupons at maturity is closest to:
explanation_en:
Assuming no default, sources of return for a bond investor include:
coupon and principal payments received on the dates agreed upon in the contract;
interest on reinvestment (ie, interest on interest) of coupons between the time each one is received and the end of the bond's holding
period; and
capital losses or gains from any sale of the bond prior to maturity.
One assumption made in calculating the YTM is that the bond's coupon payments are reinvested at the YTM rate. However, that may not be
possible if interest rates change, which often happens (ie, interest rate risk). If so, the investor's rate of return will likely not be equal to the bond's
initial YTM.
A change in the YTM for similar bonds affects the rate at which the coupons can be reinvested. In this scenario, interest rates rise, which
increases the reinvestment rate. The future value of the reinvested coupons is calculated as follows:
Since interest rates have risen, the investor's reinvested coupons are worth $21.88 at maturity.
(Choice A) $21.67 is the value of the reinvested coupon if one incorrectly assumes that the coupons are reinvested at the coupon rate of 4%.
(Choice B) $21.77 results from assuming that the coupons are reinvested at the bond's YTM rate at purchase (ie, 4.25%).

question_en: An investor buys a bond at a price below 100% of par value. The investor later sells the bond prior to maturity. The gain or loss on sale will most likely be the difference between the sale price and the:
option_b: carrying value based on straight-line amortization of the original discount.
option_c: carrying value based on the YTM at purchase and the time remaining to maturity.
explanation_en:
The capital gain or loss on a bond is usually not the difference between the purchase and sale price. The gain or loss is the difference between
the selling price and the bond's carrying value. If the purchase price is any value other than 100% of par value, the carrying value changes
over time.
For bonds purchased at a price above or below 100% of par value, the premium or discount must be amortized over the time-to-maturity. The
schedule of carrying values (ie, present values) is a trajectory of prices at which the bond would trade if its YTM were constant over the time to
maturity.
There cannot be a capital gain or loss on a bond held to maturity as the original purchase price adjusted for cumulative amortization converges
with par value (ie, pull to par). For bonds sold prior to maturity, the carrying value is determined by using the YTM at which the bond was trading
when purchased to discount the coupons and principal over the remaining time to maturity when the sale occurred.

question_en: A manager is concerned with identifying a noncallable coupon bond that minimizes the risk of funding a future liability. Which type of duration is most appropriate for this manager to use?
explanation_en:
Noncallable coupon bonds contain two types of interest rate risk: price risk and reinvestment risk. Interest rate changes have opposite effects on
these two risks and on the components of bond returns. Interest rate changes are:
inversely related to price since higher (lower) rates cause bond prices to decrease (increase), and
directly related to reinvestment income since higher (lower) rates cause reinvestment income to increase (decrease).
Macaulay duration is the holding period (ie, investment horizon) over which a bond's price change is equal to a change in reinvestment income,
allowing those changes to offset each other. Holding the bond over that period will balance reinvestment risk and price risk and minimize total
risk. Therefore, the return on a bond held over its Macaulay duration is equal to the bond's market discount rate (ie, YTM) when it was
purchased. Buying a bond with a Macaulay duration equal to the time until a liability is due minimizes the risk that the bond's issuer will be unable
to fund that liability.
(Choice A) Key rate duration measures the effect on bond prices of a change in one (or more) specific-term interest rate(s).
(Choice B) Modified duration measures a bond's approximate percentage price change due to a 100-basis-point change in its YTM, ignoring the
impact of convexity.

question_en: An investor buys a 20-year bond at par value. The bond pays a 4% semiannual coupon and has an approximate modified duration of 13.68. The investor sells the bond one year later after interest rates have risen by 100 basis points. Which of the following sources most likely accounts for the largest portion of the investor's holding period return?
explanation_en:
The largest component of short time horizon (eg, quarterly or annual) returns on long-maturity bonds is usually capital gains or losses driven by
changes in their yields-to-maturity. Long-maturity bonds have long durations, so their prices are highly sensitive to changes in interest rates.
Unless interest rate changes are very small (eg, 20 basis points), capital gains or losses are the largest portion of return.
Interest on interest (ie, reinvestment of coupon) income is relatively insignificant over short time horizons. Reinvestment income is earned only on
cash flows received during the holding period, and then only for the remainder of the period. In this scenario, the first coupon earns reinvestment
income over the second half of the year. Even at high reinvestment rates, reinvestment income is a small fraction of coupon income (Choice C).
Duration is a measure of a bond's price sensitivity to a change in its yield-to-maturity. Due to this bond's long approximate duration (13.68%), the
yield increase of 100 basis points (1%) would result in a capital loss of about three times the coupon income (4%). The estimated price decline is
shown in the bottom row of the table (Choice A).
Naturally, outcomes depend on specific circumstances. Coupon rates vary from 0% to over 10%. Some securities (eg, US mortgage-backed) pay
principal and interest monthly, allowing for a bigger contribution from reinvestment income. Nonetheless, in all but the most stable interest rate
environments, price changes are likely to be the largest contributor to return for long-dated bonds over short horizons.

question_en: An investor buys a previously issued bond that has 12 years remaining to maturity at a price of 92.4639 per 100 par value. The bond has an 8.0% YTM and pays a 7.0% annual coupon. Two years later the bond is sold for 96.5680 at a YTM of 7.5%. The carrying value used to determine the capital gain is closest to:
explanation_en:
The capital gain or loss on a bond is usually not the difference between the purchase and sale price. The gain or loss is the difference between
the selling price and the bond's carrying value. If the purchase price is at any value other than 100% of par value, the carrying value will
change over time.
For bonds purchased at a price above or below 100% of par, the premium or discount must be amortized over the time to maturity. This process
results in carrying value at maturity equal to 100% of par. Thus, for bonds held to maturity, there will never be a capital gain or loss.
For bonds sold prior to maturity, the carrying value is based on the YTM at the bond's purchase. The carrying value is determined by using the
YTM at the bond's purchase to discount the coupons and principal over the remaining time to maturity.
(Choice A) 93.2048 would be the carrying value if the bond paid coupons semiannually.
(Choice C) 93.7199 is the result of using straight-line amortization of the discount rather than the constant yield method.

question_en: An investor purchases a 20-year 6% annual coupon bond at 100% of par value. 10 years later the bond has a YTM of 10% and is trading at 75.42 per 100 of par value. Assuming a reinvestment rate of 10% since purchase, the largest effect on the bond's holding period rate of return is most likely the:
explanation_en:
There are three sources of return on coupon-bearing fixed-income securities:
Coupon income: annual coupon payments over the holding period
Capital gain or loss: difference between purchase price and current market value or sale price
Reinvestment income: interest earned from reinvesting the coupons received over the holding period
In this scenario, the coupon income over the holding period provides the greatest source of return (Choices A and C).
The source that has the largest impact on rate of return depends on the specific circumstances. Capital gain or loss, typically the largest factor in
the short run, results from change in a bond's YTM and, therefore, its price. Coupon income accrues at a constant rate over time and often
exceeds the price change in the long run.
Reinvestment income is not earned until after the receipt of the first coupon and therefore has a negligible impact in the short run. However, due
to compounding, reinvestment income can be the biggest factor in the long run if the reinvestment rate and coupon income are high enough.
It should be noted that reinvestment income is most efficiently calculated indirectly by calculating the future value of the coupons then subtracting
the coupon income. The calculation is illustrated using the formula for the future value of an ordinary annuity but is best solved using the time
value of money functions on a calculator.

explanation_en:
Macaulay duration is the weighted average time (in years) to receive all the future expected cash flows from a bond. Macaulay duration allows
investors to compare their exposure to reinvestment risk and price risk. Modified duration, derived from Macaulay duration, measures the
sensitivity of bond prices to changes in interest rates and is widely used to assess the interest rate risk of bonds.
For a zero-coupon bond, the Macaulay duration is simply the bond's maturity since it has only one cash flow: the principal repayment at maturity,
in this case at the end of Year 20. Since the Macaulay duration (20) is known, modified duration can be calculated as:
The denominator is the periodicity yield, the YTM divided by the coupon periodicity, which is semi-annual (ie, 2) in this instance. While it is very
likely on the exam that the question will state a periodicity, the standard convention for most zero-coupon bonds is to assume semi-annual
coupons with a periodicity of 2. Doing so allows a direct yield comparison to the vast majority of government and corporate coupon bonds, which
pay semi-annually.
(Choice A) 19.23 results from not accounting for the semiannual coupon convention.
(Choice C) 20.00 is the bond's Macaulay duration.

question_en: A callable bond's coupon rate is 100 basis points (bps) below yields-to-maturity on noncallable bonds having the same time to maturity and credit risk. If market yields decline by 200 bps, the callable bond's effective duration most likely:
explanation_en:
Duration measures bond price sensitivity to changes in interest rates. Graphically, duration is the slope of the price/yield function. The effective
duration of a callable bond decreases as market interest rates decline below its coupon rate. Callable and noncallable bond prices behave
similarly when interest rates rise (purple curve segment), but their prices and durations diverge significantly as yields fall below bond coupon rates.
A callable bond has an embedded option giving the issuer the right to purchase (ie, call) the bond prior to maturity. The further market rates drop
below a bond's coupon, the greater the likelihood it will be called. As a result, no matter how low rates fall, the potential appreciation of a callable
bond is limited. That is reflected by the flattening slope (ie, decreasing duration) of the red segment of the callable bond price/yield curve.

question_en: A corporation buys a 5-year default-risk-free government bond to fund a lump-sum liability due in five years. The bond is noncallable and pays coupons semiannually. Which of the following types of risk does the corporation most likely have the greatest exposure to?
explanation_en:
Macaulay duration is the weighted average time until receipt of the coupon and principal payments. The investment application of that insight is
that a bond's Macaulay duration is the holding period (investment horizon) over which changes in price and in reinvestment income exactly offset
one another. Thus, for holding periods equal to Macaulay duration, an investor's return is the YTM at which the bond was purchased.
Investment horizons shorter than Macaulay duration result in exposure to price risk. Investment horizons longer than Macaulay duration result
in exposure to reinvestment risk.
For coupon bonds, the Macaulay duration is always shorter than the bond's maturity. Since a liability due in five years is being funded with a
bond that has a duration of less than five years, the corporation has exposure to reinvestment risk.
(Choice A) Since the bond matures when the liability comes due, inflation will impact both equally, so the corporation has no exposure to inflation
risk.
(Choice B) Market price risk results from changes in credit quality and market yields. Buying a default risk-free security removes credit quality
concerns. Owning a security that matures at the time the liability comes due eliminates interest rate–related price risk. No matter how much
interest rates change over five years, the bond will be worth its par value at that time.

question_en: An investor buys a bond for 115.443470 per 100 par value. The bond has 10 years left until maturity, a 5% YTM, and a 7% annual coupon. Four years later, the bond is sold for 112.894681 at a YTM of 4.5%. The capital gain or loss is closest to a:
explanation_en:
The capital gain or loss on a bond trade is the difference between the selling price and the bond's carrying value, not the purchase price.
For bonds sold prior to maturity, the carrying value is the present value of the remaining cash flows, using the YTM at purchase, not the current
YTM, to discount those remaining cash flows.
Since they must converge with par value by maturity, the carrying values for bonds purchased at a premium decline over time. Although the bond
in this instance sold for less than its purchase price, its sale price was higher than its carrying value, so there is a capital gain.
(Choice A) A 2.5488 loss is the result of using the original purchase price rather than the carrying value.
(Choice C) A 3.6286 gain results from using straight-line amortization of the purchase premium to determine the carrying value.

Proceeds on disposition (price received for secondary market sale or par value at maturity)

For bonds held to maturity, three variables impact their relative contributions: time to maturity, coupon rate, and the interest rate at which coupon
payments are reinvested.

The reinvestment income is the future value of the coupons (ie, coupons plus reinvestment income) less the coupon payments. Use time value of
money functions on the calculator to compute reinvestment income:
For short- and intermediate-terms bonds, principal will be the largest component of total money return to maturity. As time to maturity lengthens,

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\7. Fixed Income\7.10 Interest Rate Risk and Return - Answers.pdf
question_en: An analyst has collected information on three bonds, each of which matures in 10 years and uses an annual compounding convention: Which of the bonds most likely has the shortest Macaulay duration?
explanation_en:
Macaulay duration is a function of maturity, coupon, and yield. It is the weighted average time until the coupons and principal are due. Each
payment is weighted by its present value as a percentage of the bond's full price.
Macaulay duration is positively related to maturity: the longer the maturity, the longer the average time to a bond's cash flows. Duration is
inversely related to coupon rate and yield. The higher the coupon, the shorter the average time until receipt of all cash flows. Higher yields
reduce present values, and that impact increases with time due to compounding over more periods, shortening the weighted average time.
An illustration of the Macaulay duration for each bond is shown below. The bonds' cash flows can be envisioned as being stacked on a weightless
balance beam whose length equals the time to maturity. The present value weighted average time is where a fulcrum would have to be located so
that the balance beam would not tilt left or right. That balance point (location of the fulcrum) is the bonds' Macaulay duration.
Since all the bonds have the same maturity and are trading at the same yield, the highest coupon bond has the shortest Macaulay duration
(Choices B and C).

question_en: A noncallable bond's approximate duration is closest to its effective duration when:
option_a: it has a long time to maturity.
option_b: its benchmark curve is relatively flat.
option_c: it is priced at a significant premium to its par value.
explanation_en:
Duration measures a bond's price sensitivity to changes in interest rates. Approximate duration (ie, approximate modified duration)
measures price sensitivity with respect to changes in a bond's YTM. Effective duration measures price sensitivity based on an identical change
in all rates of a benchmark curve. Effective duration is typically used for callable bonds, but it can also be used for noncallable bonds.
Although the formulas for approximate and effective duration are similar, they often produce different results. For an upward-sloped benchmark
curve, changing each yield by the same amount causes the corresponding spot rate to change by more than the benchmark yield. The price
obtained by discounting the bond's cash flows by the appropriate spot rates is different than the price obtained by changing the YTM, even if the
YTM and the benchmark curve are shifted by the same amount.
Approximate duration and effective duration are identical only when the benchmark curve is completely flat, which rarely occurs. Approximate
duration is closest to effective duration when:
the bond's price is close to par,
the bond has a short maturity, and/or
the benchmark curve is relatively flat.
(Choice A) When a bond's maturity is shorter, there are fewer cash flows to discount, so the difference in prices from using spot rates versus
YTM will be less than for a bond with a longer time to maturity. The smaller price differences result in the approximate duration being closer than
the effective duration.
(Choice C) When a bond's price is closer to par, it implies a smaller difference between the YTM and the spot rates constructed from a
benchmark curve. The smaller difference indicates it is likely that the curve is flatter, so the effective duration is closer to the approximate duration.

question_en: Investor X and Investor Y purchase identical bonds with 3 years until maturity, a YTM of 8.88%, an annual coupon of 6%, and a price of 92.7. After purchase and before the first coupon, the YTM for the bonds drops to 7.9% and remains at that level for the life of the bonds. Investor X's time horizon is 2 years, and Investor Y's time horizon is 3 years. Investor X's annual rate of return on investment is most likely:
option_a: less than Investor Y's rate of return.
option_b: equal to Investor Y's rate of return.
option_c: greater than Investor Y's rate of return.
explanation_en:
A bond investor's rate of return is equal to the bond's YTM if:
the issuer does not default,
the bond is held until maturity, and
the coupons are reinvested at the initial YTM.
In this scenario, since the YTM on the identical bonds changes and the investors have different time horizons, the rates of return differ. A bond's
annual rate of return is its annualized holding period return based on the sum of its reinvested coupons and its sale price:
A change in YTM affects both the coupon reinvestment rate and the price of the bond prior to maturity. In this scenario, interest rates fall,
negatively impacting the rate at which coupons can be reinvested. This disproportionately disadvantages Investor Y, who has a longer holding
period (3 years) and redeems at par; therefore, Investor Y depends more on the coupon reinvestment portion of the return. Investor Y's rate of
return (8.82%) is less than the bond's initial YTM (8.88%).
Investor X, who sells the bond before maturity and therefore has a shorter holding period, is more affected by the bond's price than the rate of
coupon reinvestment. Since interest rates decrease, the bond's price rises; therefore, Investor X is positively impacted. Investor X's rate of return
(9.28%) is greater than the bond's initial YTM (8.88%).
Investor X's rate of return is about 0.46% (9.28% − 8.82%) greater than Investor Y's rate of return (Choices A and B). The effect of a change
in interest rates on bond prices and coupon reinvestments is summarized in a table.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\7. Fixed Income\7.10 Interest Rate Risk and Return - Answers.pdf
question_en: The modified duration of a fixed-rate coupon bond with no embedded options most likely quantifies the:
option_a: sensitivity of the bond's price to a change in its YTM.
option_b: weighted average time to receipt of the bond's cash flows.
option_c: expected standard deviation of returns over the life of the bond.
explanation_en:
Modified duration quantifies the sensitivity of a bond's price to a change in its yield. Therefore, modified duration can be used to estimate a
bond's percentage price change using the formula in the exhibit. The calculated percentage price change is only an approximation. Errors in
estimates of price change arise as a result of the curvilinear relationship between price and yield (green function); duration assumes a linear
relationship.
Duration, the slope of the blue tangent line, measures the sensitivity of price to yield changes at current market values, allowing the use of
duration as a measure of risk. Duration's primary application is quantifying the sensitivity of bond prices and the value of bond portfolios to interest
rate changes.
Consider the consequence for two bonds with different durations. For equal declines in their YTM, the bond with the longer duration would have a
larger percentage price increase. If their yields rose by the same number of basis points, the longer-duration bond would have a larger
percentage price decrease.
(Choice B) Macaulay duration is usually interpreted as a measure of a bond's life. It is the present value–weighted average time until the receipt
of a bond's remaining contractual cash flows.
(Choice C) Duration is sometimes mistakenly believed to quantify bond price volatility. Volatility quantifies dispersion of outcomes (eg, returns).
Duration quantifies sensitivity, not volatility.

subtopic: 7.11 Yield-Based Bond Duration Measures and Properties
question_en: An analyst obtains the following information on a three-bond portfolio: All are fixed-rate bonds paying annual coupons, and there is no accrued interest. If the YTM on each bond increases by 10 basis points, which bond's price change is most likely to have the greatest impact on the portfolio value?
explanation_en: A bond's money duration is its annual modified duration multiplied by the bond's full price. In this calculation, the full price is the bond's market value, as none of the bonds have any accrued interest. Money duration is a measure of a bond's price sensitivity to a change in its YTM expressed in the currency units of the bond's denomination. Unlike other measures of price sensitivity (ie, modified and effective durations that estimate percentage price change, money duration estimates the total change in value. Since it is weighted by the size of the position, money duration more effectively measures the impact individual bond positions have on portfolio risk. (Choice A) Bond X is the largest position by value invested but it has a much shorter duration than the other bonds. (Choice C) Bond Z has the longest duration of the three bonds but has a much smaller weight in the portfolio than either of the other two securities.
